items.name: Aaron Levie
items.text: This wouldn’t have sounded possible a year ago, but it’s becoming much more reasonable now that you can get 10X output gains based on the latest in AI model and harness progress. The result is that teams within the same company are driving very different levels of output based on how they’ve adopted AI. This is a different phenomenon from other tech. Typically in the economy you think of technology adoption rates on a per firm basis, because the company generally adopts a relatively standardized approach to doing the new tech thing. Like “that company has gone digital or adopted the cloud”. So generally the uplift across teams is more or less the same across teams. AI is starting to look quite different. Even within the same company you can have a 10X delta between the lowest and highest adopters of AI and the impact they’re seeing. The teams that are able to actually figure out how to redesign their processes to best deploy agents in their workflows can see up to an order of magnitude jump in productivity depending on the job function. Right now this is heavily concentrated in coding, but more work will become coding adjacent so we can expect similar results elsewhere too. This is going to definitely lead to some wild dynamics within companies.

items.name: Peter Steinberger
items.text: What a year this has been! Time to reflect and do a blog post over the holidays. OC is in a great place, we found a niche in prosumer and enterprise adoption. The multiplayer team feature is best in class. Shipping reliable and free open source is also really really hard, and waking up to countless user complaints every day is an emotional challenge. I’m glad the team is taking over most of the work these days. We mostly been focussing on the boring part of ensuring things are fast, reliable and secure, with the exception of the new memory system and soon OpenClaw ID. To many more years!

items.name: Madhu Guru
items.text: the predictions around the Jensen saga were a great demo of how little correlation there is between confidence and being right. it’s wild how many prominent VCs, analysts and experts spoke with complete confidence about how things would play out . some flip-flopped on their predictions within days - each time with the same confidence! our info ecosystem asymmetrically rewards certainty, speed and brashness… “I don’t know, let’s see how this plays out” just doesn’t get eyeballs. worth remembering with ALL “expert” commentary you consume - people often have far less certainty than their tone suggests. they just form a view, stake out a position and say it loudly. take everything with a sack of salt. this news cycle was also a good way to calibrate on the people who are consistently loud and wrong.

items.name: Amjad Masad
items.text: America can build the best frontier models and still lose the global AI race. Which is why Jensen’s return matters far beyond Nvidia. Governments around the world want sovereign AI: models they can run on their own soil, on their own infrastructure, under their own control. If American companies won’t meet that demand, Chinese companies will. Countries will start with Chinese models, then adopt Chinese infrastructure and chips. Having the smartest model won’t mean much if most of the world runs on someone else’s stack. We’ve seen a version of this play out with Huawei. China understood that supplying the world’s telecom infrastructure creates lasting strategic influence. Once a country builds its networks around your equipment, it also builds technical expertise, supplier relationships, and future investment around it. Replacing that equipment becomes expensive and disruptive (the US government is now trying to finance replacement operations but it’s been difficult). That’s why Jensen’s backing of the American open-model ecosystem is so important. Open models give startups the freedom to compete and give countries a reason to build on American technology. We need both frontier leadership and global adoption. Open models are essential to getting both. https://t.co/f34FKKbljl

items.name: Peter Yang
items.text: I've been using Gemini 4 Neon and @antigravity all weekend and made a free video course on how you can get the most out of this combo. Some takeaways: 1. Orchestrator and /swarm are very useful for planning and building with multiple agents. At one point, I had 42 agents running at once. 2. /grill-me is a great built-in skill that gets Antigravity to ask clarifying questions to help you flesh out the plan first. 3. Remote control is better than Claude Code's because every thread is active by default. I show you how to add Antigravity to your phone home screen to run this in the video. 📌 Watch my full 17-minute Antigravity course here: https://t.co/lmfSTiVBsm
